blocks.text: “THE BURDEN OF THE WORD OF THE LORD TO ISRAEL BY MALACHI” (MALACHI 1:1) · EXILE & RETURN
Malachi. A dispute with priests and people, ending with Moses and Elijah.
SCRIPTURE CALLS
Prophet
ERA
Exile & return 586–430 BC
IN THE DAYS OF
No ruler named beside him
BOOK
Malachi
HOW THE WORD CAME
The book is headed “The burden of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi”, and says nothing else of him.
THE CALL
How the word came
The book is headed “The burden of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi”, and says nothing else of him. Malachi 1:1

From the textThe book is set out as a dispute: the LORD speaks, the people's objection is quoted (“Yet ye say, Wherein…?”), and the LORD answers. Malachi 1:2 Malachi 1:6 Malachi 2:14 Malachi 2:17 Malachi 3:7 Malachi 3:8 +1 more
Scholars' viewG. A. Smith (1898) notes that “Malachi” could mean “My Angel or Messenger”, the same word as in 3:1, “Behold, I send My messenger”. Malachi 1:1 Malachi 3:1 [14]
The book speaks to a people under a governor (“offer it now unto thy governor”) and with a temple and altar in use. Malachi 1:7–10 Malachi 3:1

HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
From the textScripture says nothing of Malachi beyond the heading of his book. Malachi 1:1
TRADITION SAYS

A tradition preserved in the Lives of the Prophets ascribed to Epiphanius, as the Jewish Encyclopedia reports it, makes Malachi “of the tribe of Zebulun”, born after the Captivity, and says “he died young, and was buried in his own country with his fathers”.[33] Who says so: pseudo-Epiphanius, Lives of the Prophets, as reported in the Jewish Encyclopedia, reported 1904

A rabbinic saying runs: “After the death of the last three prophets, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, the Holy Spirit departed from Israel”.[34] Who says so: Tosefta, Sotah 13.2, as quoted in the Jewish Encyclopedia, reported 1902
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
A title, “his messenger”, not a name
The Septuagint, as reported by S. R. Driver (1891) and G. A. Smith (1898)
Driver and Smith note that the Greek translators read 1:1 as “by the hand of his messenger”. Malachi 1:1 [5][14]
Ezra the scribe
The Targum of Jonathan; Joshua ben Karha in the Talmud (Megillah 15a); Jerome, who reports it

The Targum adds to “by the hand of Malachi” the words “whose name is called Ezra the scribe”. The Jewish Encyclopedia reports that Jerome knew the belief that Malachi was Ezra, and that the Talmud also records an identification with Mordecai. Driver answers that had Ezra been the author, “it is difficult to think that his authorship would have been thus concealed”.[33][5]
An official name or a title drawn from 3:1, for an anonymous book
Hengstenberg and Vitringa, as reported by C. F. Keil (1868); Ewald, Kuenen, Reuss and Stade, as listed by S. R. Driver (1891); G. A. Smith (1898)

Smith holds that “Malachi” is “an anonymous work”, and that the name “was a purely artificial one borrowed from chap. iii. 1, Behold, I send My messenger”, the title being added by the editor of the Twelve, like the headings of Zechariah 9:1 and 12:1. Malachi 3:1 Zechariah 9:1 Zechariah 12:1 [13][14][25][5]
The prophet's own name
C. F. Keil (1868)
Keil answers that the arguments for an official name “are not conclusive”: other prophets' headings also give only a name, and names of this form are common. Malachi 1:1 [25]

WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture gives Malachi no father, home, tribe or date.
Malachi names no king; he speaks only of “thy governor” (Mal 1:8).
Scripture does not say how or when Malachi died.
